summary: Language foundation for ratio and proportion (ages 9–11): children must use ratio, proportion, percentage, scale, equivalent, relative size, part-to-part, part-to-whole and 'out of' precisely, and grasp the central distinction that a RATIO compares part to part (3 red : 2 blue) while a PROPORTION compares a part to the whole (3 out of 5 are red = 3/5 = 60%). Because these words are used loosely in everyday speech and are often taught as the inseparable phrase 'ratio and proportion', the objective is to differentiate them through repeated use in concrete mixing/sharing/recipe contexts rather than through memorised definitions. The payoff is preventing the classic error of reading a part-to-part ratio as if it were a part-to-whole fraction.
misconceptions: Uses 'ratio' and 'proportion' interchangeably, as if they mean the same thing
Reads a part-to-part ratio as a part-to-whole fraction: hearing 'red to blue is 2:3' and saying '2/3 are red' (should be 2/5)
Treats 'proportion' only as everyday 'a large proportion' (a vague amount) rather than a comparison of part to whole
Confuses 'scale' / 'scale factor' with a difference (adds a fixed amount) rather than a multiplicative enlargement

activities.title: Squash-mixing bench: one mixture, two descriptions
steps: Build a mixture by adding whole 'parts' of concentrate and water into a jug (for example 1 part concentrate to 4 parts water).

As each part is added, read two pictures that update together: a twin-bar showing concentrate beside water (part to part) and a single stacked bar showing the whole mixture with the concentrate shaded (part to whole).
Complete two sentence frames about the SAME mixture: 'the RATIO of concentrate to water is __ : __' and 'the PROPORTION that is concentrate is __ out of __'.
Then 'say it another way': express the proportion as a fraction, a percentage and an 'out of' phrase (for 1 part in 5: 1/5 = 20%).
Change the recipe and say whether the ratio and the proportion change.
activities.insight: The same mixture is described two different ways depending on which picture you read: for 1 concentrate to 4 water, the 1 sits against the 4 in the twin-bar (ratio 1:4) and against the whole of 5 parts in the single bar (proportion 1 out of 5). Ratio compares part to part; proportion compares part to whole; the whole = the sum of the parts.

activities.title: 'For every' spoken frame before notation
steps: Describe a mixture aloud using 'for every' before any colon notation: 'for every 1 concentrate there are 4 water'.
Then translate the spoken frame into the ratio 1:4.
State separately how much of the WHOLE drink is concentrate: 1 out of 5.
Repeat with coloured counters or paint instead of squash to hear the same structure in a new context.
activities.insight: 'For every ___ there are ___' makes part-to-part audible before symbols are introduced, so the ratio notation is read as a comparison of parts rather than copied as a rule.

activities.title: In-role recipe talk that requires precise words
steps: Describe recipes and drink orders to an in-role partner (for example a smoothie-bar owner), using 'ratio' and 'proportion' correctly.
When the partner challenges a loose statement — 'you said proportion; did you mean part to part or part to whole?' — re-say it with the matching word.
Explain a part-to-part comparison and a part-to-whole comparison for the same order.
activities.insight: Correct USE of the vocabulary in unscripted dialogue is the actual objective; being asked to clarify loose usage forces the part-to-part vs part-to-whole reference to become explicit.

activities.title: Sort and complete: ratio vs proportion across contexts
steps: Sort statements about mixtures, recipes and beads into 'this is a ratio' vs 'this is a proportion'.
Fill in sentence frames: 'the ratio of red to blue is __ : __' and 'the proportion that is red is __ out of __'.
For a described situation such as 'red to blue is 2:3', state what proportion are red (2 out of 5) and explain why '2/3 are red' is wrong.
activities.insight: Across varied contexts the same structural distinction holds: the ratio uses the part counts; the proportion uses the whole (sum of the parts).

activities.title: Labelled mixing glossary (reference scaffold)
steps: On a worked mixing example, tap the concentrate to reveal 'part', tap the jug to reveal 'whole', and tap the pair to reveal 'ratio 1:4 / proportion 1 out of 5'.
Use it to look up which word names which comparison while doing the building or talking tasks.
activities.insight: Each term is anchored to a concrete feature of the mixture: parts, the whole, and the two comparisons built from them.

activities.title: Scale factor from an enlargement pair
steps: Compare an original shape with its enlargement and find how many times bigger every length is ('every length is 3 times as big').
State the scale factor as that multiplier ('a scale factor of 3') and check it is multiplicative, not an added amount.
Describe a reduction the same way (for example a scale factor of 1/2).
activities.insight: 'Scale'/'scale factor' names a multiplicative enlargement or reduction — every length is multiplied by the same number — not a fixed amount added on.

checkQuestion: Here's a jug of orange squash made with 1 cup of concentrate and 4 cups of water. Tell me about this drink using the words 'ratio' and 'proportion' — describe how much concentrate there is compared with the water, and how much of the whole drink is concentrate.
checkAnswer: The RATIO of concentrate to water is 1:4 (or 'for every 1 concentrate there are 4 water') — a part-to-part comparison; and the PROPORTION of the drink that is concentrate is 1 out of 5 (1/5, 20%) — a part-to-whole comparison. The two numbers (4 vs 5) differ because ratio compares part to part and proportion compares part to whole.
